1.pericope_label: Write thee all the words that I have spoken unto thee in a book
debates: How far the book Jeremiah is commanded to write extends
When the promised restoration falls, and whether any return yet granted answers to its terms
outliers: Gill refers the promise to a spiritual coming in the latter day and denies that it belongs to the first coming
Ellicott alone makes the point of the command that this prophecy was committed to writing from the first rather than spoken to the people
themes: A book laid up among the public rolls rather than a letter sent to captives
A preface set before the promises so that a stupefied people would attend
The hope of a return in two years, extinguished when the two years had gone
Exiles on the Euphrates and others yet farther off in the cities of the Medes

4.pericope_label: Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it: it is even the time of Jacob trouble; but he shall be saved out of it
debates: Whether the passage speaks of the time of the Messiah or gathers up doctrine the people had already heard
Whose voice utters the cry of trembling
Which day is the great day of trouble
outliers: Calvin denies the messianic reference here, against Jews and Christians alike, and finds them wonderfully united in a reading he judges far from the meaning of the prophet
Clarke sets the terror in the war of Cyrus against the Babylonians and then doubles the deliverance forward to those who escaped the destruction of Jerusalem
themes: A man with his hands on his loins like a woman in travail
A confession extorted from people too insensible to be frightened
A yoke broken and the bonds of the captives burst
The seventieth year set against the two years of the false prophets

9.pericope_label: I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished
debates: Who the David is that the people shall serve
Whether the promise is spiritual, civil, or still future
Why the punishment of the covenant people differs in kind from that of the nations
outliers: Calvin reads the clause about serving God and their king as the establishment of good order rather than a messianic title, holding that liberty without government would bring ruin
Clarke argues from history that no reign since the captivity answers the promise, so that the people can be a nation again only in the latter days
themes: Wild beasts wandering in forests, preferred to men living without government or laws
A wound from an enemy, and a chastisement measured out by a father
Nations made a full end of, while the scattered are only corrected
Sheep destined for the slaughter while their captors flourish in luxury

12.pericope_label: Thy bruise is incurable, and thy wound is grievous
debates: Whether the bruise is incurable or only desperate
Why the prophet dwells so long on the hopelessness of the case
Who the forgetful lovers are and why they have withdrawn
outliers: Clarke overturns the rendering of the key word on the ground that a cure is promised only a few verses later
Calvin sets aside the reading that the friends withdrew out of shame, making the verse a rebuke of the alliances the people had trusted
themes: A criminal at the judgment-seat with no advocate, and a plague-stricken man with no physician
Medicines and bandages that are nowhere to be found for binding up
Lovers who courted a nation and now look on her as smitten of God
Restoration that would be as life from the dead

15.pericope_label: For I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds, saith the Lord
debates: How far forward the promise that the devourers shall be devoured reaches
What the promise of restored health literally says
Why the complaint of the sufferer is met with a rebuke rather than comfort
outliers: Gill extends the reversal past the fall of the empire that took the people captive to later conquerors and their conquerors in turn
Calvin turns the healing promise into a test for distinguishing true heralds of favour from flatterers who bury the doctrine of repentance
themes: A wheel come full circle, the devourers devoured
A healing plaster laid on a plague-stricken sufferer
An outcast whom no man seeketh after, called a harlot forgotten
A judge who wounds and then takes up the office of a physician

18.pericope_label: And the city shall be builded upon her own heap, and the palace shall remain after the manner thereof
debates: Whether the palace that is to remain is the temple or the house of the king
What the tents stand for beside the settled dwelling-places
What former time the children are to be as
outliers: Calvin rejects the reading that makes the children as aforetime mean the age before the law was given, and refers the words to the kingdom of David instead
Clarke takes the tents for the minor dispersions and the synagogues of great cities rather than for the land itself
themes: A city rebuilt upon its own heap, on the same unexceptionable ground
Tents of the old nomadic life pitched once more in the land
Thanksgiving and the voice of those that make merry going out from the rebuilt dwellings
Rulers drawn from the midst of the people rather than set over them by conquerors

21.pericope_label: And their nobles shall be of themselves, and their governor shall proceed from the midst of them
debates: Whether the noble is a class of native rulers or one glorious ruler
Who the one is that engages his heart to approach
What the covenant formula secures beyond every other happiness
outliers: Clarke keeps the promise historical, satisfied that the governors after the return were of the people themselves
Ellicott finds in the words about approaching the germ of a king who is also a priest, entering where others could not enter
themes: A glorious one who pledges his heart as security
A king who is as it were the soul of the community
A people once called not his people, now owned again
A resurrection promised to men who were as dead in exile

23.pericope_label: The fierce anger of the Lord shall not return, until he have done it, and until he have performed the intents of his heart
debates: Why a threat of tempest follows immediately on the promise of favour
Who the wicked are on whose head the whirlwind falls
What the latter days are in which the hearers shall consider
outliers: Calvin offers two readings of the abrupt turn and will not choose between them, allowing that the threat may fall on the nations or on the people who despise the offered favour
Clarke identifies the whirlwind with a particular king and his people, where the others leave the target general
themes: A sweeping whirlwind that hurls down on the head of the wicked
A vengeance that abides rather than a blast that goes over
Wrath sent out as a messenger who does not return until his errand is done
A word that returns void neither for salvation nor for perdition
